snippet.title: The iPhone That Bent in Your Pocket
snippet.description:
When Apple launched the iPhone 6 in 2014, it introduced a larger display and an incredibly thin aluminum body. Not long after release, users began sharing photos of phones that had slightly bent after being carried in their pockets. The internet quickly gave the controversy a name: "Bendgate."

While later testing showed it took significant force to permanently bend the phone, the viral photos and videos turned Bendgate into one of the biggest product controversies in smartphone history.









#Technology #Apple #iPhone #TechHistory #TechFacts #DidYouKnow #InterestingFacts #Signal404

snippet.title: Steam Controller Drives Itself to the Charger
snippet.description:
Credit: fossprime via IG

Ray Foss built an open-source project that turns the Steam Controller's haptic vibration motors into a locomotion system - allowing the controller to navigate itself to its charging dock without any external motors, wheels, or robotic arms. An overhead camera tracks the controller's real-time position and orientation. Computer vision calculates the path to the magnetic charging puck. The software then fires precisely timed vibration pulses through the built-in haptic motors, which nudge the controller across the desk surface in the correct direction, adjusting continuously as it approaches and slowing before docking. The engineering insight here is using hardware designed for one purpose - tactile feedback - to do something it was never intended to do. Haptic motors create vibration. Vibration on a surface creates movement. Movement can be directed. That chain of logic is the entire project. It combines computer vision, browser-based hardware access, and timing precision to solve a robotics problem with parts that already existed in the device.

snippet.title: Reverse Engineering the Alphabet | Android Evolution, Digital Privacy, and Google Doodles History
snippet.description:
Android Evolution, Digital Privacy, and Google Doodles History | Reverse Engineering the Alphabet | GR Music Entertainment

The provided text details the Android version history, tracing the operating system's evolution from its 2007 beta to its current iterations. It outlines how Google transitioned from using internal code names like "Astro Boy" to a long-running confectionery-themed naming convention that ended with Android 10. The documentation highlights significant technical milestones, including the introduction of the Android Market, the shift to Material Design, and the implementation of the Android Runtime (ART). Each major release is categorized by its API level and release date, showcasing a steady progression in hardware support and user interface refinement. Additionally, the records describe essential features such as multitasking improvements, enhanced security protocols, and the development of specialized versions for wearable technology. Ultimately, these sources serve as a comprehensive chronological archive of the software's growth and its impact on the mobile industry.

snippet.description:
Turns out, not everything Apple makes on the low-end is like the MacBook Neo...
Thanks to @FitnexaAI for sponsoring this video. Check out Fitnexa SomniPods 3 here and get $10 off with coupon SNAZZY10: https://go.fitnexa.com/XMBmhF
Get your Window Cap at Copland Supply! - https://copland.supply/products/hat-2

*Buy FANTASTIC merch at Copland Supply* - https://copland.supply
Follow Snazzy Labs on Twitter - https://twitter.com/snazzylabs  
Follow me on Bluesky - https://snazzy.fm/UW
Follow me on Threads - https://snazzy.fm/XV
Follow me on Mastodon - https://snazzy.fm/NN
Follow me on Instagram - https://instagram.com/snazzyq

A complete current-generation Apple ecosystem for $1,925 — MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, base iPad, Apple Watch SE 3, and AirPods 4 — and after 30 days living on Apple's cheapest hardware, only two of the five are worth your money. The MacBook Neo genuinely surprised: 8GB of RAM handled Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, and DaVinci Resolve without a hiccup, its last-gen A-series chip runs circles around the M1 Air, and the macOS 27 Golden Gate beta made it faster, while the Apple Watch SE 3 delivers 95% of the Ultra 2 experience — always-on display, Double Tap, apnea detection without a blood oxygen sensor post-Masimo — for $219. The iPhone 17e is the disaster nobody expected: dropped frames at 60Hz, constant app relaunches, thermals so bad the display dims into unreadability outdoors, and no Apple Intelligence or new Siri in iOS 27 — a used iPhone 15 Pro at the same price is the better buy every single time. The base iPad is worse still, with decade-old silicon, a dim non-laminated display, and performance that makes the 17e look like a speed queen, while the AirPods 4 lose the seal, the bass, and Ultra Wideband Precision Finding for $30 less than AirPods Pro 3. With RAM crisis price hikes hitting Macs and iPads and Apple's new Apple Upgrade Program lease-to-own scheme designed to keep you renting forever, the real answer is buy to own — or buy used, because the magic was in the hardware all along.

A complete current-generation Apple ecosystem for $1,925 — MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, base iPad, Apple Watch SE 3, and AirPods 4 — and after 30 days living on Apple's cheapest hardware, only two of the five are worth your money. The MacBook Neo genuinely surprised: 8GB of RAM handled Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, and DaVinci Resolve without a hiccup, its last-gen A-series chip runs circles around the M1 Air, and the macOS 27 Golden Gate beta made it faster, while the Apple Watch SE 3 delivers 95% of the Ultra 2 experience — always-on display, Double Tap, apnea detection without a blood oxygen sensor post-Masimo — for $219. The iPhone 17e is the disaster nobody expected: dropped frames at 60Hz, constant app relaunches, thermals so bad the display dims into unreadability outdoors, and no Apple Intelligence or new Siri in iOS 27 — a used iPhone 15 Pro at the same price is the better buy every single time. The base iPad is worse still, with decade-old silicon, a dim non-laminated display, and performance that makes the 17e look like a speed queen, while the AirPods 4 lose the seal, the bass, and Ultra Wideband Precision Finding for $30 less than AirPods Pro 3. With RAM crisis price hikes hitting Macs and iPads and Apple's new Apple Upgrade Program lease-to-own scheme designed to keep you renting forever, the real answer is buy to own — or buy used, because the magic was in the hardware all along.
